analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal job-discrimination remedies while capping harassment awards and pushing disputes to arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 77 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to make it easier to prove job discrimination that has a disproportionate effect on a racial, ethnic, or gender group, and it would make workplace harassment—including sexual harassment—an explicit legal violation with money damages up to $150,000. It also gives workers a clearer right to sue over discrimination in contracts and in biased seniority systems, extends filing deadlines for federal employees, and for the first time would bring congressional employees under the same anti-discrimination enforcement as other federal workers. At the same time, it includes guardrails favored by employers: damages are capped, juries cannot set the dollar amounts, workers generally must try the employer's own internal complaint process first, and the bill encourages binding arbitration instead of lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination or harassment on the job. They would gain a clear statutory definition of harassment, money awards up to $150,000, expedited court relief while harassment is ongoing, and recovery of expert-witness fees. Federal employees would get more time to file and interest on delayed judgments, and congressional staff would finally be covered by the same employment-discrimination rules as everyone else.

how_it_helps.text: It writes into law the burden of proof for 'disparate impact' claims: a worker must show a practice harms a protected group, and the employer must then show it is justified by business necessity; if a comparably effective, comparable-cost alternative exists and the employer refuses it, the practice is unlawful [S2][S3].

It makes harassment because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin an unlawful employment practice, defines sexual harassment explicitly, lets courts award up to $150,000 on top of other relief, and requires expedited hearings for temporary relief while the harassment continues [S3].
It confirms the right to make and enforce contracts covers every benefit and term of the contract, and that this right is protected against private discrimination as well as state action [S2][S3].

It lets workers challenge a seniority system adopted for a discriminatory purpose even when the bias is not visible on the face of the rule, with the claim accruing when the system is adopted, when a worker becomes subject to it, or when they are injured by it [S2][S3].

It adds expert-witness fees (up to $300 per day) to the attorney's fees a prevailing worker can recover, extends the federal-employee filing window from 30 to 90 days, and requires the government to pay the same interest for delayed payment as private parties must [S2].

It replaces the exemption for the 'legislative branch' with coverage of Congress, its Houses, committees, offices, and Members' offices, with each House exercising the enforcement authority of the EEOC over its own workplace [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers—private businesses and the federal government—bear new liability for harassment and discriminatory practices, the cost of internal complaint systems, interest on delayed judgments, and litigation fees including expert witnesses. Congressional offices lose their exemption from employment-discrimination enforcement.

drawbacks.text: Monetary awards for harassment are capped at $150,000 total, and in no case can a jury consider, recommend, or determine the amount of that award—leaving the size of compensation in a judge's hands [S3].

A harassment claim fails if the worker did not use the employer's own internal complaint procedure within 90 days, a precondition that depends on the employer having built an effective process in the first place [S3].

The bill encourages binding arbitration in place of court resolution where parties knowingly and voluntarily agree, which for many employees would mean a private, judge-less forum decided under the employer's chosen process [S3].

Its definition of 'justified by business necessity' is lenient—a practice qualifies if the employer's legitimate goals are 'significantly served' by it, not only if the practice is required for the job—making it easier for employers to justify practices with discriminatory effects [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real gains for discrimination and harassment victims—explicit statutory protections, interim court relief, and fee recovery—but deliberately trades away the strongest remedies. The $150,000 cap, the ban on juries setting damages, the mandatory internal-complaint step, and the arbitration language were designed to keep litigation costs predictable for employers. A worker with catastrophic harassment damages would be limited by the cap; a worker who skipped the internal process within 90 days could lose the claim entirely; and the lenient business-necessity standard makes it easier for employers to defend practices with biased effects. It is a help-to-workers bill built with employer safeguards built in, which is why it drew business-friendly backing even as it expanded workers' rights.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to a civil rights subcommittee, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Representative Robert Michel of Illinois, the House Republican Leader, introduced the bill on March 12, 1991, joined by 77 cosponsors—all of them Republicans [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to both the House Committee on Education and Labor and the House Committee on Judiciary [S5].
On April 16, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill never reached the House floor for any vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead in the narrow sense that they were never subject to this bill's remedies, and congressional offices kept their exemption from anti-discrimination enforcement. In the broader 1991 civil rights fight, Congress did enact a Civil Rights Act that November blending elements of the competing Democratic and Republican bills, so many workers' gains similar to this bill's did reach law—but this particular bill itself died without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 77 cosponsors were Republicans and none were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled committees never acted on the bill; there were no roll-call votes.

industries.note: The bill creates new liability for harassment and discriminatory practices, but it caps damages at $150,000, keeps damages decisions out of juries, requires workers to use internal complaint systems, and encourages arbitration—guardrails businesses sought in the 1991 civil rights debate. Workers gain remedies; employers gain limits on how much those remedies can cost.

Federal agencies would face a 90-day filing window for workers' claims and must pay interest on delayed judgments, matching what private parties owe. Those costs exist to compensate federal workers for discrimination they suffer.

industries.industry: Congress as an employer (Members' offices and committees)
industries.note: The bill strips the legislative branch's exemption and gives each House EEOC-style enforcement authority over its own offices, subjecting congressional employers to the same rules as everyone else. Officeholders' loss here is accountability for their own staff workplaces.
Prevailing workers could recover expert fees up to $300 per day on top of attorney's fees, and new harassment claims and interim-relief hearings would generate more civil rights litigation work.
